section.title: By Faith
section.sectionRationale: Having said the righteous will live by faith, the writer now parades the great cloud of witnesses, from creation to the prophets, who lived and died by faith. Each acted on God's word about things unseen, longing for a better, heavenly country. Together they show what faith is and does, yet they did not receive the promise apart from us, for God had planned something better in Christ.
section.thesis: Faith is the assurance of what is hoped for and the conviction of what is not seen; from Abel to the prophets, the ancients were commended for such faith, obeying God's word, enduring suffering, and longing for a better country, yet none received the promise in full, for God planned that only together with us, in Christ, would they be made perfect.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the definition of faith; the faith of the first ancestors, Abel, Enoch, and Noah; the faith of Abraham and Sarah; the faith of the patriarchs and Moses; faith that conquered and faith that suffered; and the better thing God planned for all His people together.

verses.text: Now {{pistis|faith}} is the {{hypostasis|assurance}} of what we hope for and the {{elenchos|certainty}} of what we do not see.
This is why the ancients were {{martyreo|commended}}.
By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.
By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts. And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.
By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death: “He could not be found, because God had taken him away.” For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.
And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.
By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family. By faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

units.label: Abraham and Sarah
units.note: looking for the city with foundations

verses.text: By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.
By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise.
For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.
By faith Sarah, even though she was barren and beyond the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised.
And so from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.

All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.
Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own.
If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return.
Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son,
even though God had said to him, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.”
Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.
By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future.
By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff.
By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.
By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict.
By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.
He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.
He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward.
By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; he persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn.

units.label: Faith that conquered and faith that suffered
units.note: the world was not worthy of them

verses.text: By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days.
By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.
And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets,
who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions,
quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight.
Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection.
Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment.
They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated.
The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground.
These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised.
God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust that takes God at His word. The keyword of the chapter, repeated as a refrain: 'by faith' each person acted on God's promise about things unseen, and by such faith they were commended and lived.

hypostasis.gloss: Assurance, substance, the firm ground under something. Faith gives present substance and reality to what is hoped for, so that the future promise becomes a settled confidence on which one can stand and act.

elenchos.gloss: Conviction, proof, certainty. Faith is the inner certainty and evidence of realities that cannot be seen, treating God's unseen promises as sure and proven because God has spoken.

martyreo.gloss: To bear witness, to testify, and in the passive to be commended or well attested. The ancients were commended by God through their faith; Scripture bears witness to them, and their example bears witness to us.

basic.context: After saying the righteous live by faith, the writer shows what that looks like across the whole Old Testament. He defines faith, then walks through hero after hero, from Abel to the prophets, each acting on God's word about things they could not yet see. Some conquered kingdoms; others were tortured and killed. All were commended for their faith, yet none received the full promise in their lifetime, because God planned that they and we would be made complete together in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the repeated 'by faith' as the drumbeat of the chapter. Faith here is not vague optimism but taking God at His word about unseen realities and acting on it. The list is selective and moves toward its climax: they looked for a better, heavenly country, and were not made perfect apart from us.
basic.originalLanguages: Faith, pistis, is the hypostasis, assurance or substance, of what we hope for and the elenchos, conviction, of what we do not see. By such faith the ancients were martyreō, commended, attested by God.
basic.typology: Many episodes foreshadow Christ: Abel's better sacrifice, Isaac received back as from death, the Passover blood, the better resurrection. Moses valued disgrace for Christ, showing the ancients' faith was ultimately faith in the coming Redeemer.
basic.christ: The faith of all these witnesses was oriented, however dimly, toward the promise fulfilled in Christ. Moses esteemed disgrace for Christ; all died looking for what only Christ brings, and only in Him are they and we made perfect together.
basic.god: God rewards those who earnestly seek Him and is not ashamed to be called the God of these pilgrims, for He has prepared a city for them. God planned something better, that all His people across the ages would be perfected together.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis records Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and Sarah. Exodus tells of Moses and the Passover. Joshua recounts Jericho and Rahab. Hebrews 12 draws the application.
basic.oneStory: The whole Old Testament is a story of people living and dying by faith in promises they did not see fulfilled; that story reaches its goal in Christ, in whom the promise comes and all the faithful are made perfect together.

context.literary:
Hebrews 11 is one long sentence of testimony built on a refrain. 'By faith' opens eighteen separate verses, and the unmistakable beat gives the chapter its sense of a procession. The writer is not writing a catalogue for its own sake. He is writing an extended illustration of the line he has just quoted, 'My righteous one will live by faith,' 10:38, and the whole chapter is a series of cases showing what that living looks like.

The chapter is built in clear stages. Verses 1 to 3 define faith and place it at the very start, with creation. Verses 4 to 7 give three figures from before the flood: Abel, Enoch and Noah. Verses 8 to 22 are devoted to the patriarchs, with Abraham and Sarah taking by far the most space, and Isaac, Jacob and Joseph following in a few quick lines. Verses 23 to 31 handle Moses and the conquest, and verses 32 to 38 break into a rapid summary where the names run out, 'Time will not allow me,' and the focus shifts from named people to deeds and then to unnamed sufferers. Verses 39 and 40 draw the lesson.

Two verses close earlier sections and are worth marking. Verses 13 to 16 interrupt the story of Abraham to explain the common direction of all the patriarchs: they died without receiving what was promised because they were seeking a country of their own, a better one. The writer pauses the parade to say where it is going. At the end, verses 35 to 38 turn sharply from triumph to torment with the little word 'others,' so that the reader sees victory and suffering placed side by side as equal expressions of faith.

The chapter also has a literary frame. It begins with a statement about things unseen, verse 1, and the last word is about being made perfect, verse 40. Everything in between is a movement from the seen to the unseen, and from the individual to the whole company.
context.historical:
The readers needed these stories because they were tempted to measure their faith by outcomes. They had lost property, endured public shame and watched friends go to prison, 10:32-34. A people in that position can easily conclude that if God were pleased with them things would go better. The writer answers by walking them through the Scriptures they already knew, where some of the people God commended died without seeing the promises fulfilled.

The examples are drawn from the whole sweep of the Old Testament as the Jewish believers knew it. Abel, Enoch and Noah belonged to the stories in Genesis 4 to 6. The patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, and the writer takes their lives in order, with an eye on their final words, since Isaac, Jacob and Joseph are each remembered for something they said or ordered near death, verses 20 to 22. The exodus period is told through Moses' parents and Moses himself, and the conquest through Jericho and Rahab. The judges and kings come in a run of names in verse 32.

Verses 33 to 38 compress later history. The mouths shut of lions recall Daniel, Daniel 6:22, and the quenched fire recalls his three friends in Daniel 3. The women who received back their dead recall the stories of Elijah and Elisha, 1 Kings 17:17-24 and 2 Kings 4:32-37. Some readers think the 'tortured' and the 'sawed in two' may refer to martyrs of the second century before Christ, when the Maccabean revolt began, because the verb for 'tortured' is used of the torment of the faithful Jews under Antiochus. The 'sawed in two' is not recorded in the Old Testament and may come from Jewish tradition, so we should speak of it cautiously. The writer's readers would not have needed a source.

The picture of strangers and exiles in verse 13 is rooted in the actual social position of the patriarchs. They were resident aliens with no land of their own, so that Abraham, after Sarah died, had to ask the Hittites for a place to bury her, Genesis 23:4. The first readers, believers in a hostile city, would have read themselves into that picture.
context.canonical:
Hebrews 11 is the New Testament's great chapter on faith, and it handles the Old Testament in a way that shapes how the church reads it. The writer does not treat the earlier Scriptures as a set of rules replaced by a better system. He treats them as a record of people who lived by the same trust that Christians now live by, and he reads the stories as already pointing forward.

The chapter depends on Genesis 15:6, 'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness,' which Paul turned into his argument for justification by faith in Romans 4 and Galatians 3. Where Paul draws out that faith, not works, is the way a person is counted righteous, Hebrews draws out that faith is a way of walking, a life shaped by the promise. James takes up yet a third angle in James 2:21-23, saying faith is shown by what it does. Together they form a coherent picture. Faith receives, faith lives and faith acts.

Within the New Testament, the chapter is a bridge. It stands directly after the quotation of Habakkuk 2:4, and it leads into the call to run in 12:1-2. The 'cloud of witnesses' that opens chapter 12 is the gallery of chapter 11. Its definition of faith also stands next to Paul's remark that 'we walk by faith, not by sight,' 2 Corinthians 5:7.

The chapter's last note, that the Old Testament believers have not yet been made perfect without us, gives the canon a unity. The church does not replace Israel's faithful ones, and they do not stand apart from the church. They share one hope and one destiny. Jesus says something close in John 8:56, 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad,' and Hebrews supplies the longer story behind that remark.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to see that faith is the ordinary way of life for the people of God, not an exceptional feat reserved for the heroic. By beginning with a general statement and then moving through names, he shows that the faith he asks of them is the faith that every earlier generation was asked for. The people who built, left, hid, crossed and endured were not different in kind from the readers; they were people with the same promises and fewer clues.

He wants them to see that faith looks beyond the visible. Each of the examples is described as responding to something not yet seen, a flood, an inheritance, a son, an exodus, a reward. The common thread is that these people took God's word as more real than their circumstances. The readers, facing circumstances that seemed to say God had abandoned them, are meant to take courage from the fact that the same was true of those who went before.

Third, he wants them to understand that faith includes both victory and loss. The chapter does not allow a prosperity reading. It gives the walls of Jericho and the sword's edge, the lions' mouths and the sheepskins and caves. The writer insists that the ones who were stoned and sawn in two had the same faith as those who conquered kingdoms, and the world was not worthy of either.

Finally, he wants them to feel the weight of verse 40. Their own place in the story is not that of late arrivals but of the people for whom the whole line of faith had been waiting. God had planned something better, and the readers are in the generation that sees Christ. That is a reason not to shrink back, since to turn away now would be to drop the baton at the very moment the saints of all the ages are looking on.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what these people did and what happened to them. It does not command every believer to repeat their actions. Nobody is told to build an ark, sacrifice a son or leave their country on an unmarked road. The examples are given to illustrate a posture, not to supply a list of deeds. What is prescribed is faith itself: the habit of trusting God's word about what is unseen and acting accordingly.

The text is also careful about what it does not promise. Verses 33 to 35a describe deliverances, and verses 35b to 38 describe sufferings, and the writer calls both equally the fruit of faith. A reader who concludes from the first half that faith always rescues, or from the second that faith always costs, has misread the chapter. The common ground is that all were commended and none received the promise in full.

The passage also describes some people with real flaws. Samson and Jephthah are on the list, and Rahab is named by her past. The chapter does not endorse everything they did. It commends the faith that shaped the best of what they did, and in that sense it holds out hope to ordinary believers. The commendation is for trusting God, not for flawless conduct.

A final care is needed with the verb tenses of verse 13. 'All these people died in faith' describes what the patriarchs did. The writer's readers are to infer that faith can hold to the end without sight, and that is a prescription in the form of an example.

debates.question: Is the faith of the Old Testament saints the same faith that saves under the new covenant?

views.label: One faith, differently informed
views.case: The ancients trusted God's promises about the unseen, looking forward to what Christ would bring, while believers now trust the same God in the light of Christ's finished work; it is one saving faith with a shared object, the God of the promise. Paul makes the same point in Romans 4, where Abraham is the father of all who believe.

views.label: Faith oriented to the promise, fulfilled in Christ
views.case: Their faith reached toward realities not yet revealed, and verse 40 shows they are made perfect only together with us in Christ, so their faith and ours meet in the one Redeemer to whom all the promises pointed. Moses' valuing of 'disgrace for Christ,' verse 26, suggests the writer thinks of Christ as the hidden object of their hope.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter unites the whole people of God in one faith and one destiny, with Christ as the point where the two meet.

debates.question: Does verse 1 describe faith as a settled inner confidence, or as something objectively real that faith holds?

views.label: Subjective assurance
views.case: The BSB takes the word often translated 'substance' as 'assurance,' meaning the inner confidence of a person who trusts what is promised. This fits the surrounding use of the same word at 3:14, where the writer speaks of holding to the confidence we had at first, and it fits the examples that follow, each of which is about someone trusting and acting.

views.label: Objective reality or title deed
views.case: Others take the word to mean that faith gives real existence, in a present form, to what is hoped for, like a deed that already secures a property not yet occupied. On this reading faith is not merely a feeling about the future but a present grasp of a promise that is already guaranteed. A similar sense of firm foundation appears in the word's wider use.

debates.bearing: The two readings agree that faith is not wishful thinking. The examples that follow all show people committing themselves on the strength of God's word, and verse 6 grounds that in belief that God exists and rewards those who seek Him.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 says that the universe was 'formed' at God's command. The Greek verb is katartizo, the same word that appeared at 10:5 for the body 'prepared' for the Son. It means to fit together, to put in order, and it is also used of mending nets, Matthew 4:21. The creation is pictured as a fitted work, assembled by a word. The word behind 'command' is rhema, a spoken word, not the more common logos. The universe came from something said, which is the faith of Genesis 1: God spoke and it was so.

Verse 5 says Enoch 'was taken up,' and the BSB footnote notes the Greek is literally 'transferred.' The verb is metatithemi, to move from one place to another, and it is the same verb the writer uses at 7:12 for a change of priesthood. Genesis 5:24 in the Greek Old Testament says Enoch 'was well pleasing to God' where the Hebrew says he 'walked with God,' and Hebrews picks up the Greek phrase in the second half of the verse: before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God. The same family of words returns in verse 6, 'without faith it is impossible to please God.'

In verse 7 Noah was 'warned,' from chrematizo, a word for receiving a divine oracle or instruction, and moved 'in godly fear,' eulabeia, a reverent caution. Both words are the writer's own and set the tone for the chapter: faith responds to a word from God and does so reverently.

Verses 9 and 13 give the patriarchs' condition. Abraham 'dwelt as a stranger,' using the verb paroikeo, from paroikos, a resident alien with no rights of land. In verse 13 they confessed themselves 'strangers and exiles,' xenoi and parepidemoi. The pairing recalls Genesis 23:4, where Abraham says to the Hittites that he is a foreigner and an outsider among them, and Peter later takes the same word for the church, 1 Peter 2:11. In verse 13 they also 'welcomed' the promises from afar, aspazomai, a word of greeting, as one waves to a ship still far off.

Verse 19 says Abraham 'reasoned' that God could raise the dead, using logizomai, to calculate or reckon. It is the same verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 15:6 for faith 'credited' as righteousness. The faith is not blind: Abraham worked out a conclusion from what he knew of God. The writer adds that he received Isaac back 'in a sense,' and the Greek is en parabole, in a figure or likeness. The word is the root of 'parable.' Isaac's return was a picture of resurrection before there was a resurrection. The same verb for 'received' is komizo, and the writer uses it carefully.

That verb matters in verses 33 and 39. Verse 33 says some 'gained what was promised,' a verb of obtaining, epitynchano, which the writer also uses of Abraham at 6:15. Verse 39 says 'they did not receive what was promised,' using komizo in the sense of carrying off the final prize. The writer is not contradicting himself. Some obtained particular promises, such as a son, a land, a deliverance, but none carried off the great promise, the heavenly city and the perfecting.

In verse 26 Moses valued 'the disgrace of Christ,' oneidismos. The same word reappears at 13:13, 'bearing the disgrace He bore.' In verse 35 the 'tortured' are from tympanizo, a verb from the word for a drum, picturing being stretched and beaten. Verse 40 uses the verb teleioo, 'to be made perfect,' which carries the sense of reaching the goal the letter has been building toward, and it recalls 10:14, where Christ's offering made the sanctified perfect for all time.

typology.type: Abel's blood that still speaks, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 4:10 records that the voice of Abel's blood cried out from the ground, and Hebrews hears it still speaking. Its cry was for justice. In Christ the pattern is raised: Hebrews 12:24 says His sprinkled blood 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.' Abel's blood called for vengeance, and the blood of Jesus speaks forgiveness. The correspondence is of a righteous man whose death speaks. The type falls short in that Abel was a victim, and his death only cried out, while Christ is a priest, and His death answers the cry.

typology.type: Isaac received back as from the dead, verses 17 to 19
typology.fulfillment: Abraham raised the knife over his one and only son, and received him back. Hebrews calls it a figure, en parabole, of resurrection. The pattern is of a beloved son given up on a mountain with wood carried for the offering, Genesis 22:6, and a substitute provided, Genesis 22:13. In Christ the father does not stay the hand: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and the Son rose on the third day. The type falls short because Isaac did not die, and so he could not redeem anyone; Christ died in fact and rose in fact.

typology.type: The Passover blood and the Red Sea, verses 28 and 29
typology.fulfillment: The blood on the doorposts meant that the destroyer passed over, Exodus 12:13, and the sea opened to bring Israel out of slavery. Paul says the fathers were 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:2, and he calls Christ our Passover lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The correspondence is of deliverance through blood and water. In Christ the escalation is from rescue from one oppressor to rescue from sin and death. The type falls short because the Passover had to be kept every year, while Christ was sacrificed once.

typology.type: Moses and the disgrace of Christ, verses 24 to 26
typology.fulfillment: Moses gave up the status of a prince's son to share the lot of slaves, and the writer calls this valuing the disgrace of Christ. The pattern is a deliverer who leaves a palace to stand with the oppressed. Paul says of Jesus that though He was in the form of God, He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-8. The correspondence is of a rescuer who chooses humiliation for the people's sake. The type is imperfect because Moses did not purchase freedom with his own life, and Moses needed deliverance himself.

typology.type: The city with foundations, verses 10 and 16
typology.fulfillment: Abraham lived in tents and looked for a city whose architect and builder is God. Zion in Jerusalem was an earthly shadow of that city, and the writer later says believers have come to 'the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22. Revelation shows the city descending with 'twelve foundations,' Revelation 21:14. The correspondence is of a permanent dwelling for the people of promise. The earthly city fell short because it could be destroyed, and the heavenly city comes from God and cannot.

study.christ:
Hebrews 11 never leaves Christ out, even though His name appears only once, in verse 26. The writer leads the reader to Him by theme, pattern and promise.

By theme, the chapter is about things not seen, and the one the readers cannot see is the Saviour. The writer says at 2:8 that we do not yet see everything subject to Him, and at 12:2 he tells the readers to fix their eyes on Jesus. Faith in this chapter is the ordinary way people respond to the unseen, and for the readers that means responding to the unseen Son at the right hand of God. Peter says of believers that though they have not seen Him they love Him, 1 Peter 1:8, and the language fits.

By pattern, the heroes all live out in part what Christ lives out perfectly. Abel's righteousness and speaking blood are fulfilled in the Righteous One, whose blood speaks a better word, 12:24. Noah's building and condemning of the world foreshadow the one who builds the church and who judges the world. Abraham's willingness to give up his son and receive him back in a figure meets its answer in the Father who gave up His Son and raised Him. Moses' choice to endure disgrace with God's people is the pattern the writer says Christ lived to the full.

The one place the name appears, verse 26, is the most surprising. Moses 'valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt.' The writer is saying that the reproach Moses bore was the same reproach that the Messiah would bear, and that Moses, in some real sense, looked to Him. Jesus said something parallel: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day,' John 8:56. The patriarchs and prophets were not simply waiting for an unknown deliverer; they were looking at a promise that was Christ in advance. Peter says the prophets inquired about the person and time to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing, 1 Peter 1:10-11.

By promise, the last verses are about Christ. 'God had planned something better for us' is the plan that centres on Him. The writer has already said that Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, 8:6, and the sacrifice that perfects, 10:14. Verse 40 says the earlier generation are made perfect together with us, and we know by whom: by the single offering of 10:14. The saints of every age depend on the same work.

The caution is that the chapter should not be turned into a hunt for Christ in every detail. Rahab's scarlet cord and Gideon's fleece are not codes. What the writer shows is that faith has always been directed to God's word, and that God's word has always reached for the Christ. The link is in the direction of the whole line, which ends in Him and in the finished work that completes the people of faith.
study.god:
This chapter says several things about God that shape how we worship Him.

He is the speaker whose word makes things. Verse 3 grounds everything in the claim that the universe was formed at His command. The chapter begins with a word and ends with a plan, and between the two is a God who speaks to Noah, calls Abraham, makes promises to Sarah and Moses. Faith, in this chapter, is the answer to a God who has first spoken.

He is a God who rewards. Verse 6 says that anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. The sentence puts together two things that are often thought to conflict: God's complete otherness, in that He is unseen and must be believed in, and His closeness, in that He pays attention to the search of ordinary people. He is not a distant first cause; He is a rewarder.

He is not ashamed. Verse 16 says that God is not ashamed to be called their God. It is a startling phrase when we remember who these people were: tent dwellers, fugitives, people who died without seeing what they were promised. The God of the whole earth takes His name from them, as He did at the burning bush, 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' Exodus 3:6. Hebrews 2:11 says Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers. The pattern runs through the letter: shame belongs to the world's estimate, not to God's.

He is a God who prepares. 'He has prepared a city for them,' verse 16, and the city's architect and builder is God, verse 10. He is not only the one who directs the journey but the one who builds the destination. The promises have been waiting, and God has kept their fulfilment in His own hand.

He is a God who keeps His people through suffering. The last section is hard. It says that some were delivered and some were not, and that the world was not worthy of the ones who suffered. The God of this chapter does not explain every case, but He commends all of them, and He holds the final reward. He does not promise that faith will be rescued from every trouble, and He does promise that none of it is wasted.

He is also a God who plans together. Verse 40 says that He planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect. God keeps the whole people in view, and He will not complete one generation's story apart from another's. The old saints wait for us, and we wait with them, and the perfecting is a shared event at the end.

For worship, the chapter calls for trust that rests on who God is rather than on what we can see, and for the humility of those who know that their story is part of a larger one. We praise a God who is faithful to the people of every age and not ashamed of any who trust Him.

crossReferences.note: The story behind verse 4. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and God looked with favour on his offering, while Cain's was not accepted. After Abel's death the voice of his blood cries out from the ground. Hebrews hears that cry as the speaking of verse 4.

The short account of Enoch, who walked with God and then was no more, because God took him. It supplies the basis of verse 5. The Greek translation renders walking with God as pleasing God, which Hebrews uses to define Enoch's faith.

Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. The founding statement about faith in the Old Testament. Hebrews 11 is largely an extended illustration of what believing the LORD looks like in the life of a person and a family.
Abraham, burying Sarah, says he is a foreigner and an outsider. This is the source of 'strangers and exiles' in verse 13. The patriarch confesses by his own mouth that this world is not his home.

Abraham tells his servants that the boy and he will go and worship, and then they will return to them. It is the sentence that supports verse 19: he spoke as one who expected to come back with his son.
The blood on the houses causes the destroyer to pass over. It is the background to verse 28, where the sprinkling of blood is an act of faith. The people stayed under the blood and were spared.

Elijah raises the widow's son at Zarephath, and the boy is given back to his mother. It is one of the stories behind verse 35, 'Women received back their dead.' The Shunammite's son in 2 Kings 4 is the other.

The chapter that follows declares that believers have already come to the city of the living God and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect. It shows the fulfilment of the perfecting awaited in 11:40, and speaks of the blood that speaks better than Abel's.

Paul describes Abraham's faith with his body as good as dead and Sarah's womb lifeless, fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. It matches Hebrews 11:11 and 12 and shows the same Abraham seen from the side of justification.

The letter's last chapter picks up the language of 11:26 and 11:10 together. Believers bear the disgrace Christ bore, and look for the city that is to come. The pilgrim theme of chapter 11 becomes the practical way of life.

Paul says, 'For we walk by faith, not by sight.' It is a compact version of Hebrews 11:1 and of the whole chapter. Both writers see the Christian life as one lived on the strength of a word rather than on what is visible.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is a story of promise. From Genesis 3:15 onward God keeps saying that something is coming, and people keep having to decide what to do in the meantime. Hebrews 11 is the place where Scripture itself looks back over that stretch and names how the faithful decided: they trusted, and they acted on what they could not see.

The list begins with creation, the first thing that faith grasps, and moves forward through the great turning points. After the fall come Abel and Enoch, the first to be commended in a world that had already broken. Noah crosses the flood. Abraham is called out of Ur and made the father of a promised family, and from him the line runs through Isaac and Jacob to Joseph, who dies asking that his bones go with Israel. In Moses the promise becomes an exodus and the long road to a land. Rahab shows that the story's circle is wider than Israel's bloodline. The judges, the kings and the prophets show it moving through Israel's own history of failure and recovery.

The chapter answers what the story had been asking. Why did the great ones of the Old Testament die with a land half-held and a promise half-kept? The answer is that they were looking for something larger. The promises to Abraham of land and offspring pointed beyond Canaan to a city whose builder is God. That reading is not forced onto them by the New Testament; it is what Abraham was doing when he lived in tents.

The passage also sets up the church's own place. Verse 40 says the saints of old are waiting to be made perfect with us. The story has a single finale and the whole people of God will enter it together. That is why chapter 12 begins with the cloud of witnesses and the call to run. We are the last leg of a relay that began in Eden.

The story ends where the chapter points. Revelation shows the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, Revelation 21:2, with foundations bearing the names of the apostles, Revelation 21:14, and gates inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel, Revelation 21:12. The patriarchs who lived in tents have a home, the saints who were destitute have a city, and the people of every age, perfected together, see the face of the one in whom they trusted without having seen.

quiz.q: How does the chapter define faith?

options.text: The assurance of what we hope for and the conviction of what we do not see.
A vague hope that things will work out.
options.note: Faith here is settled assurance grounded in God's word, not vague optimism.

options.text: Belief only in what can be proven by sight.
options.note: Faith is precisely the conviction of what is not seen.

options.text: Confident trust that God will keep His promises.
options.note: This is true and near the mark; the precise definition is the assurance of what we hope for and the conviction of what we do not see.

quiz.q: What did the pilgrims of faith long for, according to verses 13 to 16?

options.text: A better country, a heavenly one, the city God has prepared.
options.note: They sought a heavenly homeland, not the land they had left.

options.text: A homeland and city of their own.
options.note: True, they sought a country of their own, which the passage specifies is a better, heavenly one that God has prepared.

options.text: Wealth and comfort in this life.
options.note: They confessed they were strangers and exiles, longing for the heavenly city.
Their longing was for God's prepared city, not political power.

quiz.q: What surprising thing did faith lead some to endure, in verses 35 to 38?

options.text: Torture, mocking, imprisonment, and death, refusing release for a better resurrection.
options.note: Faith led not only to victories but to great suffering.

options.text: Great victories such as conquering kingdoms and shutting lions' mouths.
options.note: Faith did bring such triumphs in verses 33 to 34, but the surprising point is that the same faith also led others to torture and death.

options.text: A quiet life free of any hardship.
options.note: Many suffered greatly; the world was not worthy of them.
Some escaped by faith, but others endured suffering and death by the same faith.

quiz.q: Why did none of the ancients receive the promise in full?

options.text: Because God planned something better, that they and we would be made perfect together in Christ.
Because the promise awaited its fulfillment in Christ.
options.note: This is right in substance; verse 40 explains that God planned for them and us to be made perfect together in Christ.
God planned something better; He did not forget.

options.text: Because the promise was never real.
options.note: The promise is real and is fulfilled in Christ, uniting them with us.

questions: Faith is the assurance of what we hope for. Where is God asking you to act on His word about something you cannot yet see?
The pilgrims confessed they were strangers and exiles longing for a better country. How does living for the heavenly city change your grip on this world's comforts?
Faith led some to great victories and others to great suffering. How does this guard you against thinking faith always brings an easy life?
Moses valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt. What treasures are you tempted to prize above faithfulness to Christ?
The faithful of every age are made perfect together with us in Christ. How does belonging to this great company encourage you to keep believing?

translationNotes.note: 'Assurance' renders hypostasis, which can mean substance or firm confidence; faith gives present reality to future hopes. 'Certainty' renders elenchos, conviction or proof of the unseen.
'Disgrace for Christ' reads the Messiah into Moses' experience; the reproach the people of God bore anticipated the reproach borne by and for the Christ to come.
'Sawed in two' reflects a tradition about the death of Isaiah; the catalogue of sufferings in verses 35 to 38 likely includes the martyrdoms of the Maccabean period.
